**Given:** \(n = 27\), \(r = 0.1\) mm \(= 1 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(T = 0.072\) N/m.
**Radius of the single drop.** Volume is conserved when the droplets coalesce:
\(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 27 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \qquad \therefore R = (27)^{1/3} r = 3r = 3 \times 10^{-4}\) m
**Areas.** A liquid drop has one surface, so
initial area \(= 27 \times 4\pi r^2 = 27 \times 4\pi \times \left(10^{-4}\right)^2 = 3.393 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
final area \(= 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi \times \left(3 \times 10^{-4}\right)^2 = 1.131 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
decrease in area \(= dA = 4\pi\left(27r^2 - R^2\right) = 4\pi\left(27 \times 10^{-8} - 9 \times 10^{-8}\right) = 2.262 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
**Change in surface energy.**
\(\Delta E = T \times dA = 0.072 \times 2.262 \times 10^{-6}\)
\(\Delta E = 1.629 \times 10^{-7}\) J \(= 1.629\) erg
The surface energy **decreases** by \(1.629 \times 10^{-7}\) J. Since the area gets smaller, no work has to be done on the drops: this energy is **released to the surroundings**, mostly as heat, which is why a coalescing spray warms very slightly.

[Textbook misprint: the question also prints a specific gravity of mercury, \(\rho_{Hg}/\rho_w = 13.6\), which has nothing to do with water escaping from a dam and is not used anywhere in the book's own solution. Given
\(T = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m
Initial radius of bubble \(= 0\) cm
Final radius of bubble, \(r = 1\) cm \(= 0.01\) m
Initial surface area of soap bubble \(= 0\)
(A soap bubble has two surfaces, outer surface and inner surface).
Final surface area of soap bubble is,
\(A = 2 \times (4\pi r^2) = 8\pi r^2\)
\(\therefore\) change in area \(= dA = A - 0 = 8\pi r^2 = 0.002513\) m\(^2\)
\(\therefore\) work done \(= T \times dA = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.2513 \times 10^{-2} = 6.283 \times 10^{-5}\) J

**What is capillarity?**

Capillarity, or capillary action, is the rise or fall of a liquid inside a tube of very fine bore when the tube is dipped into the liquid. Which of the two happens depends on whether the liquid wets the tube: a liquid that wets it, such as water in glass, has an acute angle of contact and a concave meniscus and its level rises, while a liquid that does not wet it, such as mercury in glass, has an obtuse angle of contact and a convex meniscus and its level falls. The rise or fall is given by

\( h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r \rho g} \)

**Two applications of capillarity.**

(i) Oil rises through the fine pores of the wick of a lamp and reaches the flame, so the lamp keeps burning.

(ii) Water and the minerals dissolved in it rise from the roots of a tree to its topmost leaves through the fine capillaries of the stem.

**Work done in blowing the soap bubble.**

**Given:** radius of the bubble \( r = 0.1 \) m, surface tension of the soap solution \( T = 30 \) dyne/cm \( = 30 \times \frac{10^{-5}}{10^{-2}} = 0.03 \) N/m.

A soap bubble has two surfaces, an outer one and an inner one, so the area created in blowing it up from nothing is

\( dA = 2 \times 4 \pi r^{2} = 8 \pi r^{2} = 8 \times 3.142 \times \left( 0.1 \right)^{2} = 0.2514 \) m\( ^{2} \)

The work done is stored in these two new surfaces as surface energy,

\( W = T \times dA = 0.03 \times 0.2514 \)

\( \therefore W = 7.54 \times 10^{-3} \) J

Check: since \( W = 8 \pi T r^{2} \) grows as the square of the radius, a bubble of half this radius would need a quarter of the work, \( 1.885 \times 10^{-3} \) J, which is consistent with the value found.

**Given:** surface tension of the soap solution \( T = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \) N/m. The bubble is blown up from nothing, so the initial radius is 0 and the final radius is \( r = 1 \) cm \( = 0.01 \) m.

**Increase in surface area.** A soap bubble has two surfaces, an outer one and an inner one, so the total surface area of a bubble of radius \( r \) is

\( A = 2 \times \left( 4 \pi r^{2} \right) = 8 \pi r^{2} \)

The initial surface area is zero, so the whole of this area is newly created:

\( dA = 8 \pi r^{2} - 0 = 8 \times 3.142 \times \left( 0.01 \right)^{2} = 2.514 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{2} \)

**Work done.** The work done in blowing the bubble is stored in the two new surfaces as surface energy,

\( W = T \times dA = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 2.514 \times 10^{-3} \)

\( \therefore W = 6.284 \times 10^{-5} \) J

Check: \( W = 8 \pi T r^{2} \) grows as the square of the radius, so blowing the bubble on to a radius of 2 cm would take four times as much work, \( 2.514 \times 10^{-4} \) J, which is consistent with the value found.

**Given:** \(R = 2\) cm \(= 0.02\) m, \(T = 0.07\) N/m.
A **soap bubble has two free surfaces** (an inner and an outer one), so the area created in blowing it from nothing is twice the area of a sphere:
\(dA = 2 \times 4\pi R^2 = 8\pi R^2\)
\(dA = 8 \times 3.142 \times (0.02)^2 = 8 \times 3.142 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 1.0054 \times 10^{-2}\) m\(^2\)
The work done is stored as surface energy:
\(W = T \times dA = 0.07 \times 1.0054 \times 10^{-2}\)
\(W = 7.037 \times 10^{-4}\) J \(= 0.7038 \times 10^{-3}\) J
The work required is **\(0.7038 \times 10^{-3}\) J**.
If this were a liquid **drop** of the same radius, with only one surface, the answer would be half as much, \(3.52 \times 10^{-4}\) J.

By Wien's displacement law the peak of a blackbody's spectrum satisfies \( \lambda_{\max} T = b \), so

\( T = \dfrac{b}{\lambda_{\max}} \), with \( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K} \)

Every wavelength must first be expressed in METRES, since \( b \) is in m K.

**(a) \( \lambda_{\max} = 700 \text{ nm} = 700 \times 10^{-9} = 7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \)** (visible)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{7 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.139 \times 10^{3} = 4139 \text{ K} \)

**(b) \( \lambda_{\max} = 3 \text{ cm} = 3 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} \)** (microwave)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times 10^{-2}} = 9.657 \times 10^{-2} = 0.09657 \text{ K} \)

**(c) \( \lambda_{\max} = 3 \text{ m} \)** (short radio waves)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{3} = 9.657 \times 10^{-4} = 0.9657 \times 10^{-3} \text{ K} \)

**Answers: (a) 4139 K, (b) 0.09657 K, (c) \( 0.9657 \times 10^{-3} \) K.**

The temperatures fall as the peak wavelength rises, which is the inverse proportionality of Wien's law: a body that peaks in the visible must be thousands of kelvin, whereas one peaking in the microwave or radio region is a small fraction of a kelvin above absolute zero. Cases (b) and (c) are far colder than anything on Earth; the cosmic microwave background, at 2.7 K, peaks near 1 mm.
